question.text: In a consolidation (also called a merger of equals), where two companies combine into a single entity and both lose their separate identities, what specifically happens as a result of the transaction?

answer.text: A new company is formed; both original companies lose their identities and the old stocks are surrendered
Both original companies retain their identities under a newly formed holding company
Only the smaller company loses its identity while the larger one survives unchanged
The acquiring company loses its identity while the target company survives

explanation.text: The Logic: Page 187 of NISM Series IX (Merchant Banking, Jan 2026) defines a merger as a combination into a single entity in which one OR both companies lose identity, and explicitly states that when both lose identity a new company is formed and old stocks are surrendered. The stem now references that specific "both lose identity" sub-case (consolidation/merger of equals), so a new entity being formed is the uniquely correct outcome. The Trap: Retaining identities under a holding company describes a holding-company structure, not consolidation; "only the smaller company loses identity" describes an absorption-type merger, not a merger of equals; the acquiring company losing identity while the target survives is a reverse-merger pattern, not the consolidation defined on p.187. The audit flagged the original because the generic "merger" stem combined with "both companies lose identity" overgeneralised p.187's broader definition. Note: The original was ambiguous because the source defines a merger as "one OR both" companies losing identity, while the keyed option asserted "both", overgeneralising the source. The stem has been narrowed to the consolidation / merger-of-equals sub-case from p.187, which uniquely supports "new company is formed, both lose identity".
